     T ( a ) ≈ C +   12  π  2     ln ⁡ 2    (    ln ⁡ a  −  ∑  d ∣ a      Λ ( d )  d     )     {\displaystyle T(a)\approx C+{\frac {12}{\pi ^{2}}}\ln 2\,{\biggl (}{\ln a}-\sum _{d\mid a}{\frac {\Lambda (d)}{d}}{\biggr )}}

where Λ(*d*) is the [Mangoldt function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Mangoldt_function).[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-111)

A third average *Y*(*n*) is defined as the mean number of steps required when both *a* and *b* are chosen randomly (with uniform distribution) from 1 to *n*[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Norton_1990-110)

      Y ( n ) =   1  n  2      ∑  a = 1   n    ∑  b = 1   n   T ( a , b ) =   1 n    ∑  a = 1   n   T ( a ) .   {\displaystyle Y(n)={\frac {1}{n^{2}}}\sum _{a=1}^{n}\sum _{b=1}^{n}T(a,b)={\frac {1}{n}}\sum _{a=1}^{n}T(a).}

Substituting the approximate formula for *T*(*a*) into this equation yields an estimate for *Y*(*n*)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-112)

     Y ( n ) ≈   12  π  2     ln ⁡ 2 ln ⁡ n + 0.06.   {\displaystyle Y(n)\approx {\frac {12}{\pi ^{2}}}\ln 2\ln n+0.06.}

### Computational expense per step

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=27)]

In each step *k* of the Euclidean algorithm, the quotient *q**k* and remainder *r**k* are computed for a given pair of integers *r**k*−2 and *r**k*−1

 *r**k*−2 = *q**k* *r**k*−1 + *r**k*.

The computational expense per step is associated chiefly with finding *q**k*, since the remainder *r**k* can be calculated quickly from *r**k*−2, *r**k*−1, and *q**k*

 *r**k* = *r**k*−2 − *q**k* *r**k*−1.

The computational expense of dividing *h*-bit numbers scales as *O*(*h*(*ℓ* + 1)), where ℓ is the length of the quotient.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Knuth-257-261-92)

For comparison, Euclid's original subtraction-based algorithm can be much slower. A single integer division is equivalent to the quotient *q* number of subtractions. If the ratio of *a* and *b* is very large, the quotient is large and many subtractions will be required. On the other hand, it has been shown that the quotients are very likely to be small integers. The probability of a given quotient *q* is approximately ln |*u*/(*u* − 1)| where *u* = (*q* + 1)2.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-113) For illustration, the probability of a quotient of 1, 2, 3, or 4 is roughly 41.5%, 17.0%, 9.3%, and 5.9%, respectively. Since the operation of subtraction is faster than division, particularly for large numbers,[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-114) the subtraction-based Euclid's algorithm is competitive with the division-based version.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-115) This is exploited in the [binary version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_GCD_algorithm) of Euclid's algorithm.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-116)

Combining the estimated number of steps with the estimated computational expense per step shows that the Euclid's algorithm grows quadratically (*h*2) with the average number of digits *h* in the initial two numbers *a* and *b*. Let *h*0, *h*1, ..., *h**N*−1 represent the number of digits in the successive remainders *r*0, *r*1, ..., *r**N*−1. Since the number of steps *N* grows linearly with *h*, the running time is bounded by

      O   (    ∑  i < N    h  i   (  h  i   −  h  i + 1   + 2 )   )   ⊆ O   (   h  ∑  i < N   (  h  i   −  h  i + 1   + 2 )   )   ⊆ O ( h (  h  0   + 2 N ) ) ⊆ O (  h  2   ) .   {\displaystyle O{\Big (}\sum _{i<N}h_{i}(h_{i}-h_{i+1}+2){\Big )}\subseteq O{\Big (}h\sum _{i<N}(h_{i}-h_{i+1}+2){\Big )}\subseteq O(h(h_{0}+2N))\subseteq O(h^{2}).}

### Alternative methods

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=28)]

Euclid's algorithm is widely used in practice, especially for small numbers, due to its simplicity.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-117) For comparison, the efficiency of alternatives to Euclid's algorithm may be determined.

One inefficient approach to finding the GCD of two natural numbers *a* and *b* is to calculate all their common divisors; the GCD is then the largest common divisor. The common divisors can be found by dividing both numbers by successive integers from 2 to the smaller number *b*. The number of steps of this approach grows linearly with *b*, or exponentially in the number of digits. Another inefficient approach is to find the prime factors of one or both numbers. As noted [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#Greatest_common_divisor), the GCD equals the product of the prime factors shared by the two numbers *a* and *b*.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Schroeder_21-9) Present methods for [prime factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization) are also inefficient; many modern cryptography systems even rely on that inefficiency.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Schroeder_216-12)

The [binary GCD algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_GCD_algorithm) is an efficient alternative that substitutes division with faster operations by exploiting the [binary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_numeral_system) representation used by computers.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-119) However, this alternative also scales like [*O*(*h*²)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-O_notation). It is generally faster than the Euclidean algorithm on real computers, even though it scales in the same way.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Crandall_2001-93) Additional efficiency can be gleaned by examining only the leading digits of the two numbers *a* and *b*.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-120)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-121) The binary algorithm can be extended to other bases (*k*-ary algorithms),[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-122) with up to fivefold increases in speed.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-123) [Lehmer's GCD algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer's_GCD_algorithm) uses the same general principle as the binary algorithm to speed up GCD computations in arbitrary bases.

A recursive approach for very large integers (with more than 25,000 digits) leads to [quasilinear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasilinear_time) integer GCD algorithms,[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-124) such as those of Schönhage,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-126) and Stehlé and Zimmermann.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-127) These algorithms exploit the 2×2 matrix form of the Euclidean algorithm given [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#Matrix_method). These quasilinear methods generally scale as *O*(*h* log *h*2 log log *h*).[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Crandall_2001-93)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Moller08-94)

## Generalizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=29)]

Although the Euclidean algorithm is used to find the greatest common divisor of two natural numbers (positive integers), it may be generalized to the real numbers, and to other mathematical objects, such as [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial),[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Lang_1984-128) [quadratic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-weinberger-129) and [Hurwitz quaternions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_quaternion).[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-stillwell151-152-130) In the latter cases, the Euclidean algorithm is used to demonstrate the crucial property of unique factorization, i.e., that such numbers can be factored uniquely into [irreducible elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_element), the counterparts of prime numbers. Unique factorization is essential to many proofs of number theory.

### Rational and real numbers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=30)]

Euclid's algorithm can be applied to [real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number), as described by Euclid in Book 10 of his *[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements)*. The goal of the algorithm is to identify a real number g such that two given real numbers, a and b, are integer multiples of it: *a* = *mg* and *b* = *ng*, where m and n are [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Weil_1983-27) This identification is equivalent to finding an [integer relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_relation_algorithm) among the real numbers a and b; that is, it determines integers s and t such that *sa* + *tb* = 0. If such an equation is possible, *a* and *b* are called commensurable lengths, otherwise they are [incommensurable lengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commensurability_(mathematics)).[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-131)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-132)

The real-number Euclidean algorithm differs from its integer counterpart in two respects. First, the remainders *r**k* are real numbers, although the quotients *q**k* are integers as before. Second, the algorithm is not guaranteed to end in a finite number N of steps. If it does, the fraction *a*/*b* is a rational number, i.e., the ratio of two integers

       a b   =    m g   n g    =   m n   ,   {\displaystyle {\frac {a}{b}}={\frac {mg}{ng}}={\frac {m}{n}},}

and can be written as a finite continued fraction [*q*0; *q*1, *q*2, ..., *q**N*]. If the algorithm does not stop, the fraction *a*/*b* is an [irrational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_number) and can be described by an infinite continued fraction [*q*0; *q*1, *q*2, …].[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-133) Examples of infinite continued fractions are the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio) *φ* = [1; 1, 1, ...] and the [square root of two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root_of_2), √2 = [1; 2, 2, ...].[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-134) When applied to two arbitrary real numbers, the algorithm is unlikely to stop, since [almost all](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_all) ratios *a*/*b* of two real numbers are irrational.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-135)

An infinite continued fraction may be truncated at a step *k* [*q*0; *q*1, *q*2, ..., *q**k*] to yield an approximation to *a*/*b* that improves as k is increased. The approximation is described by [convergents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_(continued_fraction)) *m**k*/*n**k*; the numerator and denominators are coprime and obey the [recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)

          m  k      =  q  k    m  k − 1   +  m  k − 2        n  k      =  q  k    n  k − 1   +  n  k − 2   ,       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}m_{k}&=q_{k}m_{k-1}+m_{k-2}\\n_{k}&=q_{k}n_{k-1}+n_{k-2},\end{aligned}}}

where *m*−1 = *n*−2 = 1 and *m*−2 = *n*−1 = 0 are the initial values of the recursion. The convergent *m**k*/*n**k* is the best [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) approximation to *a*/*b* with denominator *n**k*:[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-136)

      |    a b   −    m  k    n  k      |  <   1  n  k   2     .   {\displaystyle \left|{\frac {a}{b}}-{\frac {m_{k}}{n_{k}}}\right|<{\frac {1}{n_{k}^{2}}}.}

### Polynomials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=31)] Main article: [Polynomial greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_greatest_common_divisor)

Polynomials in a single variable *x* can be added, multiplied and factored into [irreducible polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_polynomial), which are the analogs of the prime numbers for integers. The greatest common divisor polynomial *g*(*x*) of two polynomials *a*(*x*) and *b*(*x*) is defined as the product of their shared irreducible polynomials, which can be identified using the Euclidean algorithm.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Lang_1984-128) The basic procedure is similar to that for integers. At each step k, a quotient polynomial *q**k*(*x*) and a remainder polynomial *r**k*(*x*) are identified to satisfy the recursive equation

      r  k − 2   ( x ) =  q  k   ( x )  r  k − 1   ( x ) +  r  k   ( x ) ,   {\displaystyle r_{k-2}(x)=q_{k}(x)r_{k-1}(x)+r_{k}(x),}

where *r*−2(*x*) = *a*(*x*) and *r*−1(*x*) = *b*(*x*). Each quotient polynomial is chosen such that each remainder is either zero or has a degree that is smaller than the degree of its predecessor: deg[*r**k*(*x*)] < deg[*r**k*−1(*x*)]. Since the degree is a nonnegative integer, and since it decreases with every step, the Euclidean algorithm concludes in a finite number of steps. The last nonzero remainder is the greatest common divisor of the original two polynomials, *a*(*x*) and *b*(*x*).[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-137)

For example, consider the following two quartic polynomials, which each factor into two quadratic polynomials

         a ( x )    =  x  4   − 4  x  3   + 4  x  2   − 3 x + 14 = (  x  2   − 5 x + 7 ) (  x  2   + x + 2 )   and      b ( x )    =  x  4   + 8  x  3   + 12  x  2   + 17 x + 6 = (  x  2   + 7 x + 3 ) (  x  2   + x + 2 ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}a(x)&=x^{4}-4x^{3}+4x^{2}-3x+14=(x^{2}-5x+7)(x^{2}+x+2)\qquad {\text{and}}\\b(x)&=x^{4}+8x^{3}+12x^{2}+17x+6=(x^{2}+7x+3)(x^{2}+x+2).\end{aligned}}}

[Dividing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_long_division) *a*(*x*) by *b*(*x*) yields a remainder *r*0(*x*) = *x*3 + (2/3)*x*2 + (5/3)*x* − (2/3). In the next step, *b*(*x*) is divided by *r*0(*x*) yielding a remainder *r*1(*x*) = *x*2 + *x* + 2. Finally, dividing *r*0(*x*) by *r*1(*x*) yields a zero remainder, indicating that *r*1(*x*) is the greatest common divisor polynomial of *a*(*x*) and *b*(*x*), consistent with their factorization.

Many of the applications described above for integers carry over to polynomials.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-138) The Euclidean algorithm can be used to solve linear Diophantine equations and Chinese remainder problems for polynomials; continued fractions of polynomials can also be defined.

The polynomial Euclidean algorithm has other applications, such as [Sturm chains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm_chain), a method for counting the [zeros of a polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_of_a_function) that lie inside a given [real interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(mathematics)).[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-139) This in turn has applications in several areas, such as the [Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Routh%E2%80%93Hurwitz_stability_criterion) in [control theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_theory).[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-140)

Finally, the coefficients of the polynomials need not be drawn from integers, real numbers or even the complex numbers. For example, the coefficients may be drawn from a general field, such as the finite fields GF(*p*) described above. The corresponding conclusions about the Euclidean algorithm and its applications hold even for such polynomials.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Lang_1984-128)

### Gaussian integers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=32)] [!["A set of dots lying within a circle\. The pattern of dots has fourfold symmetry, i\.e\., rotations by 90 degrees leave the pattern unchanged\. The pattern can also be mirrored about four lines passing through the center of the circle: the vertical and horizontal axes, and the two diagonal lines at ±45 degrees\."](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Gaussian_primes.svg/250px-Gaussian_primes.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gaussian_primes.svg)Distribution of Gaussian primes *u* + *vi* in the complex plane, with norms *u*2 + *v*2 less than 500

The [Gaussian integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer) are [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) of the form *α* = *u* + *vi*, where u and v are ordinary [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-141) and i is the [square root of negative one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_unit).[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stillwell_2003-142) By defining an analog of the Euclidean algorithm, Gaussian integers can be shown to be uniquely factorizable, by the argument [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#B%C3%A9zout's_identity).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Gauss_1832-42) This unique factorization is helpful in many applications, such as deriving all [Pythagorean triples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_triple) or proving [Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_theorem_on_sums_of_two_squares).[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stillwell_2003-142) In general, the Euclidean algorithm is convenient in such applications, but not essential; for example, the theorems can often be proven by other arguments.

The Euclidean algorithm developed for two Gaussian integers α and β is nearly the same as that for ordinary integers,[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-hensley-143) but differs in two respects. As before, we set *r*−2 = *α* and *r*−1 = *β*, and the task at each step k is to identify a quotient *q**k* and a remainder *r**k* such that

      r  k   =  r  k − 2   −  q  k    r  k − 1   ,   {\displaystyle r_{k}=r_{k-2}-q_{k}r_{k-1},}

where every remainder is strictly smaller than its predecessor: |*r**k*| < |*r**k*−1|. The first difference is that the quotients and remainders are themselves Gaussian integers, and thus are [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number). The quotients *q**k* are generally found by rounding the real and complex parts of the exact ratio (such as the complex number *α*/*β*) to the nearest integers.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-hensley-143) The second difference lies in the necessity of defining how one complex remainder can be "smaller" than another. To do this, a [norm function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_(mathematics)) *f*(*u* + *vi*) = *u*2 + *v*2 is defined, which converts every Gaussian integer *u* + *vi* into an ordinary integer. After each step k of the Euclidean algorithm, the norm of the remainder *f*(*r**k*) is smaller than the norm of the preceding remainder, *f*(*r**k*−1). Since the norm is a nonnegative integer and decreases with every step, the Euclidean algorithm for Gaussian integers ends in a finite number of steps.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-144) The final nonzero remainder is gcd(*α*, *β*), the Gaussian integer of largest norm that divides both α and β; it is unique up to multiplication by a unit, ±1 or ±*i*.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-145)

Many of the other applications of the Euclidean algorithm carry over to Gaussian integers. For example, it can be used to solve linear Diophantine equations and Chinese remainder problems for Gaussian integers;[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-146) continued fractions of Gaussian integers can also be defined.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-hensley-143)

### Euclidean domains

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=33)]

A set of elements under two [binary operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operation), denoted as addition and multiplication, is called a [Euclidean domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_domain) if it forms a [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) R and, roughly speaking, if a generalized Euclidean algorithm can be performed on them.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-147)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-148) The two operations of such a ring need not be the addition and multiplication of ordinary arithmetic; rather, they can be more general, such as the operations of a [mathematical group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) or [monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoid). Nevertheless, these general operations should respect many of the laws governing ordinary arithmetic, such as [commutativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_property), [associativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_property) and [distributivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_property).

The generalized Euclidean algorithm requires a *Euclidean function*, i.e., a mapping f from R into the set of nonnegative integers such that, for any two nonzero elements a and b in R, there exist q and r in R such that *a* = *qb* + *r* and *f*(*r*) < *f*(*b*).[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-149) Examples of such mappings are the absolute value for integers, the degree for [univariate polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Univariate_polynomial), and the norm for Gaussian integers [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#Gaussian_integers).[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-150)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-151) The basic principle is that each step of the algorithm reduces *f* inexorably; hence, if f can be reduced only a finite number of times, the algorithm must stop in a finite number of steps. This principle relies on the [well-ordering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-order) property of the non-negative integers, which asserts that every non-empty set of non-negative integers has a smallest member.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-sharpe-152)

The [fundamental theorem of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic) applies to any Euclidean domain: Any number from a Euclidean domain can be factored uniquely into [irreducible elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_element). Any Euclidean domain is a [unique factorization domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_factorization_domain) (UFD), although the converse is not true.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-sharpe-152) The Euclidean domains and the UFD's are subclasses of the [GCD domains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCD_domain), domains in which a greatest common divisor of two numbers always exists.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-153) In other words, a greatest common divisor may exist (for all pairs of elements in a domain), although it may not be possible to find it using a Euclidean algorithm. A Euclidean domain is always a [principal ideal domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal_domain) (PID), an [integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain) in which every [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) is a [principal ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal).[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-154) Again, the converse is not true: not every PID is a Euclidean domain.

The unique factorization of Euclidean domains is useful in many applications. For example, the unique factorization of the Gaussian integers is convenient in deriving formulae for all [Pythagorean triples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_triple) and in proving [Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_theorem_on_sums_of_two_squares).[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stillwell_2003-142) Unique factorization was also a key element in an attempted proof of [Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_Last_Theorem) published in 1847 by Gabriel Lamé, the same mathematician who analyzed the efficiency of Euclid's algorithm, based on a suggestion of [Joseph Liouville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Liouville).[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-155) Lamé's approach required the unique factorization of numbers of the form *x* + *ωy*, where x and y are integers, and *ω* = *e*2*iπ*/*n* is an nth root of 1, that is, *ω**n* = 1. Although this approach succeeds for some values of n (such as *n* = 3, the [Eisenstein integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenstein_integer)), in general such numbers do *not* factor uniquely. This failure of unique factorization in some [cyclotomic fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_field) led [Ernst Kummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Kummer) to the concept of [ideal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_number) and, later, [Richard Dedekind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dedekind) to [ideals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)).[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-156)

#### Unique factorization of quadratic integers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=34)] [!["A set of dots lying within a circle\. The pattern of dots has sixfold symmetry, i\.e\., rotations by 60 degrees leave the pattern unchanged\. The pattern can also be mirrored about six lines passing through the center of the circle: the vertical and horizontal axes, and the four diagonal lines at ±30 and ±60 degrees\."](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Eisenstein_primes.svg/250px-Eisenstein_primes.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eisenstein_primes.svg)Distribution of Eisenstein primes *u* + *vω* in the complex plane, with norms less than 500. The number ω is a [cube root of 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_unity). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Golden_integer_primes.png/250px-Golden_integer_primes.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Golden_integer_primes.png)Golden integer units (hollow circles) and primes (filled circles), along with zero (+) and composite numbers (×), with each golden integer plotted at coordinates (*a* + *ωb*, *a* + *ω**b*). The number *ω* = (1 + √5)/2 is the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio) and *ω* = (1 − √5)/2 is its algebraic conjugate.

The [quadratic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer) rings are helpful to illustrate Euclidean domains. Quadratic integers are generalizations of the Gaussian integers in which the [imaginary unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_unit) *i* is replaced by a number ω. Thus, they have the form *u* + *vω*, where u and v are integers and ω has one of two forms, depending on a parameter D. If D does not equal a multiple of four plus one, then

     ω =   D   .   {\displaystyle \omega ={\sqrt {D}}.}

If, however, *D* does equal a multiple of four plus one, then

     ω =    1 +   D    2   .   {\displaystyle \omega ={\frac {1+{\sqrt {D}}}{2}}.}

If the function f corresponds to a [norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_norm) function, such as that used to order the Gaussian integers [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#Gaussian_integers), then the domain is known as *[norm-Euclidean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm-Euclidean_field)*. The norm-Euclidean rings of quadratic integers are exactly those where D is one of the values −11, −7, −3, −2, −1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 21, 29, 33, 37, 41, 57, or 73.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-157)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-158) The cases *D* = −1 and *D* = −3 yield the [Gaussian integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer) and [Eisenstein integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenstein_integer), respectively. The quadratic integers with *D* = 5, such that ω is the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio), are sometimes called [golden integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_integers).

If f is allowed to be any Euclidean function, then the list of possible values of D for which the domain is Euclidean is not yet known.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Clark_1994-159) The first example of a Euclidean domain that was not norm-Euclidean (with *D* = 69) was published in 1994.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Clark_1994-159) In 1973, Weinberger proved that a quadratic integer ring with *D* > 0 is Euclidean if, and only if, it is a [principal ideal domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal_domain), provided that the [generalized Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis) holds.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-weinberger-129)

### Noncommutative rings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=35)]

The Euclidean algorithm may be applied to some noncommutative rings such as the set of [Hurwitz quaternions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_quaternion).[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-stillwell151-152-130)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-bgv-160) Let α and β represent two elements from such a ring. They have a common right divisor δ if *α* = *ξδ* and *β* = *ηδ* for some choice of ξ and η in the ring. Similarly, they have a common left divisor if *α* = *dξ* and *β* = *dη* for some choice of ξ and η in the ring. Since multiplication is not commutative, there are two versions of the Euclidean algorithm, one for right divisors and one for left divisors.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-stillwell151-152-130)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-bgv-160) Choosing the right divisors, the first step in finding the gcd(*α*, *β*) by the Euclidean algorithm can be written

      ρ  0   = α −  ψ  0   β = ( ξ −  ψ  0   η ) δ ,   {\displaystyle \rho _{0}=\alpha -\psi _{0}\beta =(\xi -\psi _{0}\eta )\delta ,}

where *ψ*0 represents the quotient and *ρ*0 the remainder. Here the quotient and remainder are chosen so that (if nonzero) the remainder has *N*(*ρ*0) < *N*(*β*) for a "Euclidean function" *N* defined analogously to the Euclidean functions of [Euclidean domains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_domain) in the non-commutative case.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-bgv-160) This equation shows that any common right divisor of α and β is likewise a common divisor of the remainder *ρ*0. The analogous equation for the left divisors would be

      ρ  0   = α − β  ψ  0   = δ ( ξ − η  ψ  0   ) .   {\displaystyle \rho _{0}=\alpha -\beta \psi _{0}=\delta (\xi -\eta \psi _{0}).}

With either choice, the process is repeated as above until the greatest common right or left divisor is identified. As in the Euclidean domain, the "size" of the remainder *ρ*0 (formally, its Euclidean function or "norm") must be strictly smaller than β, and there must be only a finite number of possible sizes for *ρ*0, so that the algorithm is guaranteed to terminate.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-entgtrg-161)

Many results for the GCD carry over to noncommutative numbers. For example, [Bézout's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout's_identity) states that the right gcd(*α*, *β*) can be expressed as a linear combination of α and β.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-162) In other words, there are numbers σ and τ such that

      Γ  right   = σ α + τ β .   {\displaystyle \Gamma _{\text{right}}=\sigma \alpha +\tau \beta .}

The analogous identity for the left GCD is nearly the same:

      Γ  left   = α σ + β τ .   {\displaystyle \Gamma _{\text{left}}=\alpha \sigma +\beta \tau .}

Bézout's identity can be used to solve Diophantine equations. For instance, one of the standard proofs of [Lagrange's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange's_four-square_theorem), that every positive integer can be represented as a sum of four squares, is based on quaternion GCDs in this way.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-entgtrg-161)

  [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Euclid%27s_algorithm_Book_VII_Proposition_2_3.svg/330px-Euclid%27s_algorithm_Book_VII_Proposition_2_3.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Euclid's_algorithm_Book_VII_Proposition_2_3.svg)Euclid's method for finding the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two starting lengths BA and DC, both defined to be multiples of a common "unit" length. The length DC being shorter, it is used to "measure" BA, but only once because the remainder EA is less than DC. EA now measures (twice) the shorter length DC, with remainder FC shorter than EA. Then FC measures (three times) length EA. Because there is no remainder, the process ends with FC being the GCD. On the right [Nicomachus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomachus)'s example with numbers 49 and 21 resulting in their GCD of 7 (derived from Heath 1908:300).

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **Euclidean algorithm**,[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-1) or **Euclid's algorithm**, is an efficient method for computing the [greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor) (GCD) of two [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integers), the largest number that divides them both without a [remainder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remainder). It is named after the ancient Greek [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [Euclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid), who first described it in [his *Elements*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements) (c. 300 BC). It is an example of an *[algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm)*, and is one of the oldest algorithms in common use. It can be used to reduce [fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraction_(mathematics)) to their [simplest form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_fraction), and is a part of many other number-theoretic and cryptographic calculations.

The Euclidean algorithm is based on the principle that the greatest common divisor of two numbers does not change if the larger number is replaced by its difference with the smaller number. For example, 21 is the GCD of 252 and 105 (as 252 = 21 × 12 and 105 = 21 × 5), and the same number 21 is also the GCD of 105 and 252 − 105 = 147. Since this replacement reduces the larger of the two numbers, repeating this process gives successively smaller pairs of numbers until the two numbers become equal. When that occurs, that number is the GCD of the original two numbers. By [reversing the steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#B%C3%A9zout's_identity) or using the [extended Euclidean algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Euclidean_algorithm), the GCD can be expressed as a [linear combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination) of the two original numbers, that is the sum of the two numbers, each multiplied by an [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) (for example, 21 = 5 × 105 + (−2) × 252). The fact that the GCD can always be expressed in this way is known as [Bézout's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout's_identity).

The version of the Euclidean algorithm described above—which follows Euclid's original presentation—may require many subtraction steps to find the GCD when one of the given numbers is much bigger than the other. A more efficient version of the algorithm shortcuts these steps, instead replacing the larger of the two numbers by its remainder when divided by the smaller of the two (with this version, the algorithm stops when reaching a zero remainder). With this improvement, the algorithm never requires more steps than five times the number of digits (base 10) of the smaller integer. This was proven by [Gabriel Lamé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Lam%C3%A9) in 1844 ([Lamé's Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lam%C3%A9%E2%80%99s_Theorem)),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-3) and marks the beginning of [computational complexity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory). Additional methods for improving the algorithm's efficiency were developed in the 20th century.

The Euclidean algorithm has many theoretical and practical applications. It is used for reducing [fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraction_(mathematics)) to their [simplest form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreducible_fraction) and for performing [division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_(mathematics)) in [modular arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic). Computations using this algorithm form part of the [cryptographic protocols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptographic_protocol) that are used to secure [internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet) communications, and in methods for breaking these cryptosystems by [factoring large composite numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization). The Euclidean algorithm may be used to solve [Diophantine equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_equation), such as finding numbers that satisfy multiple congruences according to the [Chinese remainder theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem), to construct [continued fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction), and to find accurate [rational approximations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation) to real numbers. Finally, it can be used as a basic tool for proving theorems in [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) such as [Lagrange's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange's_four-square_theorem) and the [uniqueness of prime factorizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic).

The original algorithm was described only for natural numbers and geometric lengths (real numbers), but the algorithm was generalized in the 19th century to other types of numbers, such as [Gaussian integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer) and [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) of one variable. This led to modern [abstract algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra) notions such as [Euclidean domains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_domain).

Background: greatest common divisor

# Background: greatest common divisor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=1)] Main article: [Greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor)

The Euclidean algorithm calculates the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two [natural numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number) a and b. The greatest common divisor g is the largest natural number that divides both a and b without leaving a remainder. Synonyms for GCD include *greatest common factor* (GCF), *highest common factor* (HCF), *highest common divisor* (HCD), and *greatest common measure* (GCM). The greatest common divisor is often written as gcd(*a*, *b*) or, more simply, as (*a*, *b*),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-4) although the latter notation is ambiguous, also used for concepts such as an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) in the [ring of integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_integers), which is closely related to GCD.

If gcd(*a*, *b*) = 1, then a and b are said to be [coprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime_integers) (or relatively prime).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-5) This property does not imply that a or b are themselves [prime numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-6) For example, 6 and 35 factor as 6 = 2 × 3 and 35 = 5 × 7, so they are not prime, but their prime factors are different, so 6 and 35 are coprime, with no common factors other than 1.

 [!["Tall, slender rectangle divided into a grid of squares\. The rectangle is two squares wide and five squares tall\."](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/24x60.svg/250px-24x60.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:24x60.svg)A 24×60 rectangle is covered with ten 12×12 square tiles, where 12 is the GCD of 24 and 60. More generally, an *a*×*b* rectangle can be covered with square tiles of side-length c only if c is a common divisor of *a* and *b*.

Let *g* = gcd(*a*, *b*). Since a and b are both multiples of g, they can be written *a* = *mg* and *b* = *ng*, and there is no larger number *G* > *g* for which this is true. The natural numbers m and n must be coprime, since any common factor could be factored out of m and n to make g greater. Thus, any other number c that divides both a and b must also divide g. The greatest common divisor g of a and b is the unique (positive) common divisor of a and b that is divisible by any other common divisor c.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-7)

The greatest common divisor can be visualized as follows.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-8) Consider a rectangular area a by b, and any common divisor c that divides both a and b exactly. The sides of the rectangle can be divided into segments of length c, which divides the rectangle into a grid of squares of side length c. The GCD g is the largest value of c for which this is possible. For illustration, a 24×60 rectangular area can be divided into a grid of: 1×1 squares, 2×2 squares, 3×3 squares, 4×4 squares, 6×6 squares or 12×12 squares. Therefore, 12 is the GCD of 24 and 60. A 24×60 rectangular area can be divided into a grid of 12×12 squares, with two squares along one edge (24/12 = 2) and five squares along the other (60/12 = 5).

The greatest common divisor of two numbers a and b is the product of the prime factors shared by the two numbers, where each prime factor can be repeated as many times as it divides both a and b.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Schroeder_21-9) For example, since 1386 can be factored into 2 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 11, and 3213 can be factored into 3 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 17, the GCD of 1386 and 3213 equals 63 = 3 × 3 × 7, the product of their shared prime factors (with 3 repeated since 3 × 3 divides both). If two numbers have no common prime factors, their GCD is 1 (obtained here as an instance of the [empty product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empty_product)); in other words, they are coprime. A key advantage of the Euclidean algorithm is that it can find the GCD efficiently without having to compute the prime factors.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-11) [Factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization) of large integers is believed to be a computationally very difficult problem, and the security of many widely used [cryptographic protocols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptographic_protocol) is based upon its infeasibility.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Schroeder_216-12)

Another definition of the GCD is helpful in advanced mathematics, particularly [ring theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_theory).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Leveque_p33-13) The greatest common divisor g of two nonzero numbers a and b is also their smallest positive integral linear combination, that is, the smallest positive number of the form *ua* + *vb* where u and v are integers. The set of all integral linear combinations of a and b is actually the same as the set of all multiples of g (mg, where m is an integer). In modern mathematical language, the [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) generated by a and b is the ideal generated by g alone (an ideal generated by a single element is called a [principal ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal), and all ideals of the integers are principal ideals). Some properties of the GCD are in fact easier to see with this description, for instance the fact that any common divisor of a and b also divides the GCD (it divides both terms of *ua* + *vb*). The equivalence of this GCD definition with the other definitions is described below.

The GCD of three or more numbers equals the product of the prime factors common to all the numbers,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-14) but it can also be calculated by repeatedly taking the GCDs of pairs of numbers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-15) For example,

 gcd(*a*, *b*, *c*) = gcd(*a*, gcd(*b*, *c*)) = gcd(gcd(*a*, *b*), *c*) = gcd(gcd(*a*, *c*), *b*).

Thus, Euclid's algorithm, which computes the GCD of two integers, suffices to calculate the GCD of arbitrarily many integers.

The Euclidean algorithm can be thought of as constructing a sequence of non-negative integers that begins with the two given integers      r  − 2   = a   {\displaystyle r_{-2}=a}   and      r  − 1   = b   {\displaystyle r_{-1}=b}   and will eventually terminate with the integer zero:     {  r  − 2   = a ,    r  − 1   = b ,    r  0   ,    r  1   ,   ⋯ ,    r  n − 1   ,    r  n   = 0 }   {\displaystyle \{r_{-2}=a,\ r_{-1}=b,\ r_{0},\ r_{1},\ \cdots ,\ r_{n-1},\ r_{n}=0\}}   with      r  k + 1   <  r  k   .   {\displaystyle r_{k+1}<r_{k}.}   The integer      r  n − 1     {\displaystyle r_{n-1}}   will then be the GCD and we can state      gcd  ( a , b ) =  r  n − 1   .   {\displaystyle {\text{gcd}}(a,b)=r_{n-1}.}   The algorithm indicates how to construct the intermediate remainders      r  k     {\displaystyle r_{k}}   via [division-with-remainder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_division) on the preceding pair     (  r  k − 2   ,    r  k − 1   )   {\displaystyle (r_{k-2},\ r_{k-1})}   by finding an integer quotient      q  k     {\displaystyle q_{k}}   so that:

      r  k − 2   =  q  k   ⋅  r  k − 1   +  r  k    , with      r  k − 1   >  r  k   ≥ 0.   {\displaystyle r_{k-2}=q_{k}\cdot r_{k-1}+r_{k}{\text{, with }}\ r_{k-1}>r_{k}\geq 0.}

Because the sequence of non-negative integers     {  r  k   }   {\displaystyle \{r_{k}\}}   is strictly decreasing, it eventually [must terminate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-ordering_principle). In other words, since      r  k   ≥ 0   {\displaystyle r_{k}\geq 0}   for every     k ,   {\displaystyle k,}   and each      r  k     {\displaystyle r_{k}}   is an integer that is strictly smaller than the preceding      r  k − 1   ,   {\displaystyle r_{k-1},}   there eventually cannot be a non-negative integer smaller than zero, and hence the algorithm must terminate. In fact, the algorithm will always terminate at the *n*th step with      r  n     {\displaystyle r_{n}}   equal to zero.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-16)

To illustrate, suppose the GCD of 1071 and 462 is requested. The sequence is initially     {  r  − 2   = 1071 ,    r  − 1   = 462 }   {\displaystyle \{r_{-2}=1071,\ r_{-1}=462\}}   and in order to find      r  0   ,   {\displaystyle r_{0},}   we need to find integers      q  0     {\displaystyle q_{0}}   and      r  0   <  r  − 1     {\displaystyle r_{0}<r_{-1}}   such that:

     1071 =  q  0   ⋅ 462 +  r  0   .   {\displaystyle 1071=q_{0}\cdot 462+r_{0}.}

     462 =  q  1   ⋅ 147 +  r  1   .   {\displaystyle 462=q_{1}\cdot 147+r_{1}.}

This is the quotient      q  1   = 3   {\displaystyle q_{1}=3}   since     462 = 3 ⋅ 147 + 21.   {\displaystyle 462=3\cdot 147+21.}   This determines      r  1   = 21   {\displaystyle r_{1}=21}   and so the sequence is now     { 1071 ,   462 ,   147 ,    r  1   = 21 } .   {\displaystyle \{1071,\ 462,\ 147,\ r_{1}=21\}.}   The next step is to continue the sequence to find      r  2     {\displaystyle r_{2}}   by finding integers      q  2     {\displaystyle q_{2}}   and      r  2   <  r  1     {\displaystyle r_{2}<r_{1}}   such that:

     147 =  q  2   ⋅ 21 +  r  2   .   {\displaystyle 147=q_{2}\cdot 21+r_{2}.}

This is the quotient      q  2   = 7   {\displaystyle q_{2}=7}   since     147 = 7 ⋅ 21 + 0.   {\displaystyle 147=7\cdot 21+0.}   This determines      r  2   = 0   {\displaystyle r_{2}=0}   and so the sequence is completed as     { 1071 ,   462 ,   147 ,   21 ,    r  2   = 0 }   {\displaystyle \{1071,\ 462,\ 147,\ 21,\ r_{2}=0\}}   as no further non-negative integer smaller than     0   {\displaystyle 0}   can be found. The penultimate remainder     21   {\displaystyle 21}   is therefore the requested GCD:

      gcd  ( 1071 ,   462 ) = 21.   {\displaystyle {\text{gcd}}(1071,\ 462)=21.}

We can generalize slightly by dropping any ordering requirement on the initial two values     a   {\displaystyle a}   and     b .   {\displaystyle b.}   If     a = b ,   {\displaystyle a=b,}   the algorithm may continue and trivially find that      gcd  ( a ,   a ) = a   {\displaystyle {\text{gcd}}(a,\ a)=a}   as the sequence of remainders will be     { a ,   a ,   0 } .   {\displaystyle \{a,\ a,\ 0\}.}   If     a < b ,   {\displaystyle a<b,}   then we can also continue since     a ≡ 0 ⋅ b + a ,   {\displaystyle a\equiv 0\cdot b+a,}   suggesting the next remainder should be     a   {\displaystyle a}   itself, and the sequence is     { a ,   b ,   a ,   ⋯ } .   {\displaystyle \{a,\ b,\ a,\ \cdots \}.}   Normally, this would be invalid because it breaks the requirement      r  0   <  r  − 1     {\displaystyle r_{0}<r_{-1}}   but now we have     a < b   {\displaystyle a<b}   by construction, so the requirement is automatically satisfied and the Euclidean algorithm can continue as normal. Proof of validity

# Proof of validity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=4)]

The existence of a step     N   {\displaystyle N}   such that      r  N   = 0   {\displaystyle r_{N}=0}   follows from the condition      |   r  i    |  <  |   r  i − 1    |    {\displaystyle |r_{i}|<|r_{i-1}|}  , for     i ≥ 1   {\displaystyle i\geq 1}  . This ensures that the algorithm terminates.

The last non-zero remainder      r  N − 1     {\displaystyle r_{N-1}}   being equal to     gcd ( a , b )   {\displaystyle \gcd(a,b)}   follows from the following properties of     gcd   {\displaystyle \gcd }

1.     gcd ( x , 0 ) = x   {\displaystyle \gcd(x,0)=x}  , for all     x ≠ 0   {\displaystyle x\neq 0}  .

 In fact, the common divisors of     x   {\displaystyle x}   and     0   {\displaystyle 0}   are exactly all the divisors of     x   {\displaystyle x}  , of which     x   {\displaystyle x}   itself is the largest.

2.     gcd ( x , y ) = gcd ( y , x − z y )   {\displaystyle \gcd(x,y)=\gcd(y,x-zy)}

 In fact, the sets of common divisors of the pairs     ( x , y )   {\displaystyle (x,y)}   and     ( y , x − z y )   {\displaystyle (y,x-zy)}   are the same. In particular, the largest of their common divisors are the same. To see this, assume that     d   {\displaystyle d}   is a common divisor of     x   {\displaystyle x}   and     y   {\displaystyle y}  . This means that there are integers     X , Y   {\displaystyle X,Y}   such that     x = d X   {\displaystyle x=dX}   and     y = d Y   {\displaystyle y=dY}  . It follows that     x − z y = d X − z d Y = d ( X − z Y )   {\displaystyle x-zy=dX-zdY=d(X-zY)}  , where     X − z Y   {\displaystyle X-zY}   is an integer. Therefore,     d   {\displaystyle d}   is also a divisor of     x − z y   {\displaystyle x-zy}  . Conversely, if     d   {\displaystyle d}   is a common divisor of     x − z y   {\displaystyle x-zy}   and     y   {\displaystyle y}  , then there are integers     Z   {\displaystyle Z}   and     Y   {\displaystyle Y}   such that     x − z y = d Z   {\displaystyle x-zy=dZ}   and     y = d Y   {\displaystyle y=dY}  . From this     x = ( x − z y ) + z y = d Z + z d Y = d ( Z + z Y )   {\displaystyle x=(x-zy)+zy=dZ+zdY=d(Z+zY)}  , where     Z + z Y   {\displaystyle Z+zY}   is an integer. Therefore,     d   {\displaystyle d}   is also a common divisor of     x   {\displaystyle x}   and     y   {\displaystyle y}  .

Now, the Euclidean algorithm starts with the pair     (  r  − 2   ,  r  − 1   ) = ( a , b )   {\displaystyle (r_{-2},r_{-1})=(a,b)}   and at each step, the pair of remainders     (  r  k − 2   ,  r  k − 1   )   {\displaystyle (r_{k-2},r_{k-1})}   is replaced by     (  r  k − 1   ,  r  k − 2   −  q  k    r  k − 1   ) = (  r  k − 1   ,  r  k   )   {\displaystyle (r_{k-1},r_{k-2}-q_{k}r_{k-1})=(r_{k-1},r_{k})}  . Property 2 shows that the     gcd   {\displaystyle \gcd }   of the pairs remains invariant. In particular, the     gcd   {\displaystyle \gcd }   of the first pair     ( a , b )   {\displaystyle (a,b)}   and the last pair     (  r  N − 1   , 0 )   {\displaystyle (r_{N-1},0)}   are the same. Applying Property 1,     gcd ( a , b ) = gcd (  r  N − 1   , 0 ) =  r  N − 1     {\displaystyle \gcd(a,b)=\gcd(r_{N-1},0)=r_{N-1}}  .

Worked example

# Worked example

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=5)] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Gcd_by_long_division.svg/250px-Gcd_by_long_division.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gcd_by_long_division.svg)Calculation using repeated [long division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_division) [[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-17) [![Animation in which progressively smaller square tiles are added to cover a rectangle completely\.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Euclidean_algorithm_1071_462.gif/250px-Euclidean_algorithm_1071_462.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Euclidean_algorithm_1071_462.gif)Subtraction-based animation of the Euclidean algorithm. The initial rectangle has dimensions *a* = 1071 and *b* = 462. Squares of size 462×462 are placed within it leaving a 462×147 rectangle. This rectangle is tiled with 147×147 squares until a 21×147 rectangle is left, which in turn is tiled with 21×21 squares, leaving no uncovered area. The smallest square size, 21, is the GCD of 1071 and 462.

For illustration, the Euclidean algorithm can be used to find the greatest common divisor of *a* = 1071 and *b* = 462. To begin, multiples of 462 are subtracted from 1071 until the remainder is less than 462. Two such multiples can be subtracted (*q*0 = 2), leaving a remainder of 147:

 1071 = 2 × 462 + 147.

Then multiples of 147 are subtracted from 462 until the remainder is less than 147. Three multiples can be subtracted (*q*1 = 3), leaving a remainder of 21:

 462 = 3 × 147 + 21.

Then multiples of 21 are subtracted from 147 until the remainder is less than 21. Seven multiples can be subtracted (*q*2 = 7), leaving no remainder:

 147 = 7 × 21 + 0.

Since the last remainder is zero, the algorithm ends with 21 as the greatest common divisor of 1071 and 462. This agrees with the gcd(1071, 462) found by prime factorization [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#Background:_greatest_common_divisor). In tabular form, the steps are:

   Step *k*EquationQuotient and remainder  01071 = *q*0 462 + *r*0*q*0 = 2 and *r*0 = 147  1462 = *q*1 147 + *r*1*q*1 = 3 and *r*1 = 21  2147 = *q*2 21 + *r*2*q*2 = 7 and *r*2 = 0; algorithm ends

Visualization

# Visualization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=6)]

The Euclidean algorithm can be visualized in terms of the tiling analogy given above for the greatest common divisor.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Kimberling_1983-18) Assume that we wish to cover an *a*×*b* rectangle with square tiles exactly, where *a* is the larger of the two numbers. We first attempt to tile the rectangle using *b*×*b* square tiles; however, this leaves an *r*0×*b* residual rectangle untiled, where *r*0 < *b*. We then attempt to tile the residual rectangle with *r*0×*r*0 square tiles. This leaves a second residual rectangle *r*1×*r*0, which we attempt to tile using *r*1×*r*1 square tiles, and so on. The sequence ends when there is no residual rectangle, i.e., when the square tiles cover the previous residual rectangle exactly. The length of the sides of the smallest square tile is the GCD of the dimensions of the original rectangle. For example, the smallest square tile in the adjacent figure is 21×21 (shown in red), and 21 is the GCD of 1071 and 462, the dimensions of the original rectangle (shown in green).

Euclidean division

# Euclidean division

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=7)] Main article: [Euclidean division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_division)

At every step *k*, the Euclidean algorithm computes a quotient *q**k* and remainder *r**k* from two numbers *r**k*−1 and *r**k*−2

 *r**k*−2 = *q**k* *r**k*−1 + *r**k*,

where the *r**k* is non-negative and is strictly less than the [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value) of *r**k*−1. The theorem which underlies the definition of the [Euclidean division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_division) ensures that such a quotient and remainder always exist and are unique.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-19)

In Euclid's original version of the algorithm, the quotient and remainder are found by repeated subtraction; that is, *r**k*−1 is subtracted from *r**k*−2 repeatedly until the remainder *r**k* is smaller than *r**k*−1. After that *r**k* and *r**k*−1 are exchanged and the process is iterated. Euclidean division reduces all the steps between two exchanges into a single step, which is thus more efficient. Moreover, the quotients are not needed, thus one may replace Euclidean division by the [modulo operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo_operation), which gives only the remainder. Thus the iteration of the Euclidean algorithm becomes simply

 *r**k* = *r**k*−2 mod *r**k*−1.

Implementations

# Implementations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=8)]

Implementations of the algorithm may be expressed in [pseudocode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudocode). For example, the division-based version may be [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_programming) as[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-20)

```
function gcd(a, b)
    while b ≠ 0
        t := b
        b := a mod b
        a := t
    return a
```

At the beginning of the *k*th iteration, the variable *b* holds the latest remainder *r**k*−1, whereas the variable *a* holds its predecessor, *r**k*−2. The step *b* := *a* mod *b* is equivalent to the above recursion formula *r**k* ≡ *r**k*−2 mod *r**k*−1. The [temporary variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporary_variable) *t* holds the value of *r**k*−1 while the next remainder *r**k* is being calculated. At the end of the loop iteration, the variable *b* holds the remainder *r**k*, whereas the variable *a* holds its predecessor, *r**k*−1.

(If negative inputs are allowed, or if the `mod` function may return negative values, the last line must be replaced with `return abs(a)`.)

In the subtraction-based version, which was Euclid's original version, the remainder calculation (`b := a mod b`) is replaced by repeated subtraction.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-21) Contrary to the division-based version, which works with arbitrary integers as input, the subtraction-based version supposes that the input consists of positive integers and stops when *a* = *b*:

```
function gcd(a, b)
    while a ≠ b
        if a > b
            a := a − b
        else
            b := b − a
    return a
```

The variables *a* and *b* alternate holding the previous remainders *r**k*−1 and *r**k*−2. Assume that *a* is larger than *b* at the beginning of an iteration; then *a* equals *r**k*−2, since *r**k*−2 > *r**k*−1. During the loop iteration, *a* is reduced by multiples of the previous remainder *b* until *a* is smaller than *b*. Then *a* is the next remainder *r**k*. Then *b* is reduced by multiples of *a* until it is again smaller than *a*, giving the next remainder *r**k*+1, and so on.

The recursive version[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-22) is based on the equality of the GCDs of successive remainders and the stopping condition gcd(*r**N*−1, 0) = *r**N*−1.

```
function gcd(a, b)
    if b = 0
        return a
    else
        return gcd(b, a mod b)
```

(As above, if negative inputs are allowed, or if the `mod` function may return negative values, the instruction `return a` must be replaced by `return max(a, −a)`.)

For illustration, the gcd(1071, 462) is calculated from the equivalent gcd(462, 1071 mod 462) = gcd(462, 147). The latter GCD is calculated from the gcd(147, 462 mod 147) = gcd(147, 21), which in turn is calculated from the gcd(21, 147 mod 21) = gcd(21, 0) = 21.

Method of least absolute remainders

# Method of least absolute remainders

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=9)]

In another version of Euclid's algorithm, the quotient at each step is increased by one if the resulting negative remainder is smaller in magnitude than the typical positive remainder.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Ore_least_abs_remainders-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stewart_1964-24) Previously, the equation

 *r**k*−2 = *q**k* *r**k*−1 + *r**k*

assumed that |*r**k*−1| > *r**k* > 0. However, an alternative negative remainder *e**k* can be computed:

 *r**k*−2 = (*q**k* + 1) *r**k*−1 + *e**k*

if *r**k*−1 > 0 or

 *r**k*−2 = (*q**k* – 1) *r**k*−1 + *e**k*

if *r**k*−1 < 0.

If *r**k* is replaced by *e**k*. when |*e**k*| < |*r**k*|, then one gets a variant of Euclidean algorithm such that

 |*r**k*| ≤ |*r**k*−1| / 2

at each step.

[Leopold Kronecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Kronecker) has shown that this version requires the fewest steps of any version of Euclid's algorithm.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Ore_least_abs_remainders-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stewart_1964-24) More generally, it has been proven that, for every input numbers *a* and *b*, the number of steps is minimal if and only if *q**k* is chosen in order that      |    r  k + 1    r  k     |  <   1 φ   ∼ 0.618 ,   {\displaystyle \left|{\frac {r_{k+1}}{r_{k}}}\right|<{\frac {1}{\varphi }}\sim 0.618,}   where     φ   {\displaystyle \varphi }   is the [golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-25)

Historical development

# Historical development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=10)] [!["Depiction of Euclid as a bearded man holding a pair of dividers to a tablet\."](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Euklid.jpg/250px-Euklid.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Euklid.jpg)The Euclidean algorithm was probably invented before [Euclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid), depicted here holding a [compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_(drawing_tool)) in a painting of about 1474.

The Euclidean algorithm is one of the oldest algorithms in common use.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Knuth,_p._318-26) It appears in [Euclid's *Elements*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements) (c. 300 BC), specifically in Book 7 (Propositions 1–2) and Book 10 (Propositions 2–3). In Book 7, the algorithm is formulated for integers, whereas in Book 10, it is formulated for lengths of line segments. (In modern usage, one would say it was formulated there for [real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number). But lengths, areas, and volumes, represented as real numbers in modern usage, are not measured in the same units and there is no natural unit of length, area, or volume; the concept of real numbers was unknown at that time.) The latter algorithm is geometrical. The GCD of two lengths *a* and *b* corresponds to the greatest length *g* that measures *a* and *b* evenly; in other words, the lengths *a* and *b* are both integer multiples of the length *g*.

The algorithm was probably not discovered by [Euclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid), who compiled results from earlier mathematicians in his *Elements*.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Weil_1983-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Jones_1994-28) The mathematician and historian [B. L. van der Waerden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartel_Leendert_van_der_Waerden) suggests that Book 7 derives from a textbook on [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) written by mathematicians in the school of [Pythagoras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-van_der_Waerden_1954-29) The algorithm was probably known by [Eudoxus of Cnidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eudoxus_of_Cnidus) (about 375 BC).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Knuth,_p._318-26)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-30) The algorithm may even pre-date Eudoxus,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-32) judging from the use of the technical term ἀνθυφαίρεσις (*anthyphairesis*, reciprocal subtraction) in works by Euclid and [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-33) Claude Brezinski, following remarks by [Pappus of Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pappus_of_Alexandria), credits the algorithm to [Theaetetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theaetetus_(mathematician)) (c. 417 – c. 369 BC).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-34)

Centuries later, Euclid's algorithm was discovered independently both in India and in China,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stillwell,_p._31-35) primarily to solve [Diophantine equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_equation) that arose in astronomy and making accurate calendars. In the late 5th century, the Indian mathematician and astronomer [Aryabhata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata) described the algorithm as the "pulverizer",[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Tattersall,_p._70-36) perhaps because of its effectiveness in solving Diophantine equations.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-37) Although a special case of the [Chinese remainder theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem) had already been described in the *[Sunzi Suanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunzi_Suanjing)*,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-38) the general solution was published by [Qin Jiushao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_Jiushao) in his 1247 book *Shushu Jiuzhang* (數書九章 *[Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_Treatise_in_Nine_Sections)*).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-39) The Euclidean algorithm was first described *numerically* and popularized in Europe in the second edition of [Bachet's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Gaspard_Bachet_de_M%C3%A9ziriac) *Problèmes plaisants et délectables* (*Pleasant and enjoyable problems*, 1624).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Tattersall,_p._70-36) In Europe, it was likewise used to solve Diophantine equations and in developing [continued fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction). The [extended Euclidean algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Euclidean_algorithm) was published by the English mathematician [Nicholas Saunderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Saunderson),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-40) who attributed it to [Roger Cotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Cotes) as a method for computing continued fractions efficiently.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-41)

In the 19th century, the Euclidean algorithm led to the development of new number systems, such as [Gaussian integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer) and [Eisenstein integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenstein_integer). In 1815, [Carl Gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss) used the Euclidean algorithm to demonstrate unique factorization of [Gaussian integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer), although his work was first published in 1832.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Gauss_1832-42) Gauss mentioned the algorithm in his *[Disquisitiones Arithmeticae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disquisitiones_Arithmeticae)* (published 1801), but only as a method for [continued fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Stillwell,_p._31-35) [Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gustav_Lejeune_Dirichlet) seems to have been the first to describe the Euclidean algorithm as the basis for much of number theory.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-43) Lejeune Dirichlet noted that many results of number theory, such as unique factorization, would hold true for any other system of numbers to which the Euclidean algorithm could be applied.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-44) Lejeune Dirichlet's lectures on number theory were edited and extended by [Richard Dedekind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dedekind), who used Euclid's algorithm to study [algebraic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_integer), a new general type of number. For example, Dedekind was the first to prove [Fermat's two-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_theorem_on_sums_of_two_squares) using the unique factorization of Gaussian integers.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-45) Dedekind also defined the concept of a [Euclidean domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_domain), a number system in which a generalized version of the Euclidean algorithm can be defined (as described [below](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#Euclidean_domains)). In the closing decades of the 19th century, the Euclidean algorithm gradually became eclipsed by Dedekind's more general theory of [ideals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-46)

>
> "[The Euclidean algorithm] is the granddaddy of all algorithms, because it is the oldest nontrivial algorithm that has survived to the present day."
>

 — [Donald Knuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Knuth), *The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms*, 2nd edition (1981), p. 318

Other applications of Euclid's algorithm were developed in the 19th century. In 1829, [Charles Sturm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Charles_Fran%C3%A7ois_Sturm) showed that the algorithm was useful in the [Sturm chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm's_theorem) method for counting the real roots of polynomials in any given interval.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-47)

The Euclidean algorithm was the first [integer relation algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_relation_algorithm), which is a method for finding integer relations between commensurate real numbers. Several novel [integer relation algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_relation_algorithm) have been developed, such as the algorithm of [Helaman Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helaman_Ferguson) and R.W. Forcade (1979)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-48) and the [LLL algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra%E2%80%93Lenstra%E2%80%93Lov%C3%A1sz_lattice_basis_reduction_algorithm).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-50)

In 1969, Cole and Davie developed a two-player game based on the Euclidean algorithm, called *The Game of Euclid*,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-51) which has an optimal strategy.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-52) The players begin with two piles of *a* and *b* stones. The players take turns removing *m* multiples of the smaller pile from the larger. Thus, if the two piles consist of *x* and *y* stones, where *x* is larger than *y*, the next player can reduce the larger pile from *x* stones to *x* − *my* stones, as long as the latter is a nonnegative integer. The winner is the first player to reduce one pile to zero stones.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-54)

Mathematical applications

# Mathematical applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=11)]

Bézout's identity

# Bézout's identity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=12)] Main article: [Bézout's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout's_identity)

Bézout's identity states that the greatest common divisor *g* of two integers *a* and *b* can be represented as a linear sum of the original two numbers *a* and *b*.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-55) In other words, it is always possible to find integers *s* and *t* such that *g* = *sa* + *tb*.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-57)

The integers *s* and *t* can be calculated from the quotients *q*0, *q*1, etc. by reversing the order of equations in Euclid's algorithm.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-58) Beginning with the next-to-last equation, *g* can be expressed in terms of the quotient *q**N*−1 and the two preceding remainders, *r**N*−2 and *r**N*−3:

 *g* = *r**N*−1 = *r**N*−3 − *q**N*−1 *r**N*−2.

Those two remainders can be likewise expressed in terms of their quotients and preceding remainders,

 *r**N*−2 = *r**N*−4 − *q**N*−2 *r**N*−3 and *r**N*−3 = *r**N*−5 − *q**N*−3 *r**N*−4.

Substituting these formulae for *r**N*−2 and *r**N*−3 into the first equation yields *g* as a linear sum of the remainders *r**N*−4 and *r**N*−5. The process of substituting remainders by formulae involving their predecessors can be continued until the original numbers *a* and *b* are reached:

 *r*2 = *r*0 − *q*2 *r*1 *r*1 = *b* − *q*1 *r*0 *r*0 = *a* − *q*0 *b*.

After all the remainders *r*0, *r*1, etc. have been substituted, the final equation expresses *g* as a linear sum of *a* and *b*, so that *g* = *sa* + *tb*.

The Euclidean algorithm, and thus Bézout's identity, can be generalized to the context of [Euclidean domains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_domain).

Principal ideals and related problems

# Principal ideals and related problems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Euclidean_algorithm&action=edit&section=13)]

Bézout's identity provides yet another definition of the greatest common divisor *g* of two numbers *a* and *b*.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm#cite_note-Leveque_p33-13) Consider the set of all numbers *ua* + *vb*, where *u* and *v* are any two integers. Since *a* and *b* are both divisible by *g*, every number in the set is divisible by *g*. In other words, every number of the set is an integer multiple of *g*. This is true for every common divisor of *a* and *b*. However, unlike other common divisors, the greatest common divisor is a member of the set; by Bézout's identity, choosing *u* = *s* and *v* = *t* gives *g*. A smaller common divisor cannot be a member of the set, since every member of the set must be divisible by *g*. Conversely, any multiple *m* of *g* can be obtained by choosing *u* = *ms* and *v* = *mt*, where *s* and *t* are the integers of Bézout's identity. This may be seen by multiplying Bézout's identity by *m*,

 *mg* = *msa* + *mtb*.

Therefore, the set of all numbers *ua* + *vb* is equivalent to the set of multiples *m* of *g*. In other words, the set of all possible sums of integer multiples of two numbers (*a* and *b*) is equivalent to the set of multiples of gcd(*a*, *b*). The GCD is said to be the generator of the [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) of *a* and *b*. This GCD definition led to the modern [abstract algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra) concepts of a [principal ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal) (an ideal generated by a single element) and a [principal ideal domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal_domain) (a [domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_(ring_theory)) in which every ideal is a principal ideal).
